introduction_markdown:
This paper is arranged in three sections, A, B and C. Section A: answer ALL 5 questions; you will be graded for the best 4 answers. Section B: answer ALL 2 questions in this section. Section C: answer 2 questions out of 3; if you attempt more than 2 questions, only the first two will be considered. In calculations, you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage. Calculators are allowed. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

**Useful data:** relative atomic masses H = 1.0, C = 12.0, O = 16.0; 1 faraday = 96000 coulombs; molar volume of a gas at r.t.p. = 24000 cm$^3$; specific heat capacity of water = 4.2 J g$^{-1}$ $^\circ$C$^{-1}$; Avogadro number = $6.02\times10^{23}$; $0^\circ$C = 273 K.

questions.corrige_markdown:
**Thermal decomposition** is the breaking down of a compound into two or more simpler substances **by heat** (one reactant, several products).

Examples:

- Calcium carbonate (limestone) on strong heating gives calcium oxide and carbon dioxide: $\mathrm{CaCO_3} \xrightarrow{\text{heat}} \mathrm{CaO} + \mathrm{CO_2}$
- Copper (II) nitrate gives copper (II) oxide, brown nitrogen dioxide and oxygen: $2\mathrm{Cu(NO_3)_2} \xrightarrow{\text{heat}} 2\mathrm{CuO} + 4\mathrm{NO_2} + \mathrm{O_2}$
- Potassium nitrate gives potassium nitrite and oxygen: $2\mathrm{KNO_3} \xrightarrow{\text{heat}} 2\mathrm{KNO_2} + \mathrm{O_2}$

The reaction is usually endothermic. It is used to make quicklime and to prepare oxygen.

A **neutralization reaction** is the reaction of an **acid with a base (or alkali)** to give a **salt and water** only. The pH of the mixture moves towards 7 and the reaction is exothermic.

Examples:

- $\mathrm{HCl} + \mathrm{NaOH} \rightarrow \mathrm{NaCl} + \mathrm{H_2O}$
- $\mathrm{H_2SO_4} + 2\mathrm{NaOH} \rightarrow \mathrm{Na_2SO_4} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}$
- $2\mathrm{HNO_3} + \mathrm{CuO} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu(NO_3)_2} + \mathrm{H_2O}$

In ionic form, the essential change is $\mathrm{H^+(aq)} + \mathrm{OH^-(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{H_2O(l)}$. Uses: titration, treating acid soil with lime, indigestion tablets.

**Addition polymerization** is the reaction in which a large number of small **unsaturated molecules (monomers, containing a $\mathrm{C{=}C}$ double bond)** join together to form a very long chain molecule, the **polymer**, with **no other product** formed. The double bond opens up and each monomer links to the next.

Examples:

- Ethene gives poly(ethene): $n\,\mathrm{CH_2{=}CH_2} \rightarrow [\mathrm{CH_2{-}CH_2}]_n$
- Chloroethene gives poly(chloroethene) (PVC): $n\,\mathrm{CH_2{=}CHCl} \rightarrow [\mathrm{CH_2{-}CHCl}]_n$
- Propene gives poly(propene): $n\,\mathrm{CH_2{=}CHCH_3} \rightarrow [\mathrm{CH_2{-}CH(CH_3)}]_n$

Conditions: high pressure and a catalyst. Products are plastics used for bags, pipes and insulation.

A **substitution reaction** is one in which **an atom (or group of atoms) in a molecule is replaced by another atom (or group)**. It is typical of saturated hydrocarbons (alkanes).

Example: methane and chlorine in **ultraviolet light** (or sunlight):

$\mathrm{CH_4} + \mathrm{Cl_2} \xrightarrow{\text{UV light}} \mathrm{CH_3Cl} + \mathrm{HCl}$

One hydrogen atom of methane is replaced by a chlorine atom (chloromethane). With more chlorine the replacement continues:
$\mathrm{CH_3Cl} + \mathrm{Cl_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{CH_2Cl_2} + \mathrm{HCl}$, and so on up to $\mathrm{CCl_4}$.

Other example: ethane and bromine in light, $\mathrm{C_2H_6} + \mathrm{Br_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{C_2H_5Br} + \mathrm{HBr}$.
